extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans of British television comedy, and researchers/critics of TV humour
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article summarising the British mockumentary sitcom People Just Do Nothing: its premise, characters, production, episodes, reception and influence. Not a how-to or formal rubric but contains evaluative comments from critics about what makes the show work.

rubrics_metrics.name: humour_is_in_the_hopelessness
rubrics_metrics.description: "You don't need to know anything about garage to get it; the humour is in the hopelessness." (Jamie Clifton, Vice) — comedy arises from characters' pathetic/failed ambitions rather than insider musical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Grindah proclaims "We're going global" while broadcasting to a tiny area; the humour comes from the disparity between their grandiosity and actual reach. Anti-pattern: relying on specialist in-jokes that require knowledge of garage music rather than character-driven hopelessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: comedy_from_inability_to_read_scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every character is really, quite comfortingly, dense, and their inability to read scenarios correctly is the source of nearly all the comedy." (Rachel Aroesti, The Guardian)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/Examples: Scenes where characters misinterpret social cues, plans go wrong because of basic misunderstandings (e.g., Chabuddy's schemes ending in disaster). Scoring note: higher comedic value if misreading leads to escalating embarrassment; lower if it feels mean-spirited rather than character-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: believability_of_characters
rubrics_metrics.description: "Despite its larger-than-life characters, People Just Do Nothing’s success lies in its believability ... You get the feeling that if you drove out to Brentford you might actually run in to them." (David Renshaw, The Guardian)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Authentic detail, natural dialogue and lifelike motivations increase believability. Example: grounded domestic details (jobs, relationships) that anchor the absurdity. Anti-pattern: caricatured performances that break immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: characters_inflated_sense_of_talent
rubrics_metrics.description: All of the characters have an inflated sense of their own talent and success; they are "super confident; they’re just not good at what they do." (Steve Stamp quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How this functions: the contrast between self-perception and reality is a recurring comedic engine (e.g., Grindah proclaiming musical genius while being ignored). Use as a device to create irony and cringe. Anti-pattern: if characters show real competence without the delusion, the premise weakens.

rubrics_metrics.name: balance_of_comedy_and_pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: The show "decided to go for the dramatic jugular. The final episode of this series offered fans a precious opportunity to laugh and cry at exactly the same time ... By making you care about the characters ... viewers will now have two reasons for tuning in." (Rachel Aroesti, The Guardian)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Effective episodes mix humour with emotional stakes (e.g., Steves' grief over his nan). Scoring note: episodes that generate genuine empathy alongside jokes rate higher for overall impact; anti-pattern: jokes that undercut all emotional beats leaving characters uninvestable.

rubrics_metrics.name: improvisation_and_writing_style
rubrics_metrics.description: All episodes are written by Mustafa and Stamp, but the cast are given freedom to improvise their dialogue; by the third series Mustafa estimated material was "70/30 percent improvised."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Improvisation contributes to naturalistic performances and unexpected comic beats. Example: cast "snapping into" character after years of playing them. Production note: requires skilled actors who know their characters well; anti-pattern: excessive improvisation without editorial shaping can lead to uneven pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: mockumentary_format_and_technique
rubrics_metrics.description: People Just Do Nothing is a mockumentary in which the characters give interviews to the camera and are taped in a loose, documentary fashion; an off-screen interviewer is occasionally heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Use of talking-head interviews, fly-on-the-wall scenes, and pseudo-documentary camerawork supports both humour and realism. Example: direct-to-camera confessionals reveal delusion. Anti-pattern: inconsistent use of format that confuses tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: authentic_local_voice_and_slang
rubrics_metrics.description: The dialogue is often heavy with 21st century London slang; locations and dialect derive from Brentford/West London upbringing of creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Authentic regional language and specifics (e.g., references to local estates, jobs, slang) enhance realism and character. Accessibility note: while authentic, use should not exclude audiences (see accessibility criterion). Anti-pattern: stereotypical or lazy use of dialect that feels inauthentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: comedic_timing_and_beats
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beats are hit and joke quotas filled, scene in, scene out." (Rachel Aroesti) — the series follows traditional comedic structure with well-timed beats and reliably delivered jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Tight scene construction and timing (setup/payoff) increase joke density and viewer satisfaction. Example: scenes that build to a humiliating but well-structured punchline. Anti-pattern: meandering scenes without clear beats reduce comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: accessibility_to_non-specialist_audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "You don't need to know anything about garage to get it" — the show is accessible to viewers unfamiliar with the subculture it portrays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: While rooted in pirate radio/garage culture, humor is character-driven and broadly understandable; avoid relying solely on insider references. Scoring note: broader accessibility increases potential audience and critical praise; anti-pattern: jokes that require niche knowledge to appreciate.

rubrics_metrics.name: influences_and_cringe_comedy_lineage
rubrics_metrics.description: The show is heavily influenced by The Office, This Is Spinal Tap, Alan Partridge, Ali G and other cringe/mocumentary traditions; comparisons include a 'David Brent'–style mortifying delusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Drawing on cringe and mockumentary precedents means employing mortification, embarrassment and character self-delusion as comedic tools. Example: Grindah as a 'David Brent with malicious intent.' Anti-pattern: copying predecessor devices without fresh character or context.
